overview.text: Cinema Rex was a movie theater in Abadan, Iran, where arson killed hundreds of people on August 19, 1978. The attack occurred during growing opposition to Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and revolutionary figures accused his government and its SAVAK security agency of causing the fire. Later testimony and research identified Hossein Takb'alizadeh and several associates as participants in setting it. A special tribunal tried defendants after the 1979 revolution, but the role of any wider organizers remained contested and was not fully investigated in court. The tragedy became a powerful symbol in the struggle over who was responsible for violence before the revolution.

key_facts.text: Cinema Rex was in Abadan, an Iranian city.
The fire occurred on August 19, 1978.
Contemporary opponents of the shah publicly blamed his government and SAVAK.
Hossein Takb'alizadeh acknowledged participating in the arson at a 1980 tribunal.
Published accounts disagree about the death toll; hundreds died.

overview.text: Otto I, often called Otto the Great, was a ruler whose victories helped build a powerful kingdom in medieval central Europe. In 955 his forces defeated Hungarian, or Magyar, raiders at the Battle of Lechfeld. That success strengthened his standing among the German duchies. Pope John XII crowned him emperor in Rome on February 2, 962, linking his kingship to the western imperial title and the defense of the Latin Church. Later historians treat this coronation as a starting point for the Holy Roman Empire, although the empire's familiar name developed afterward. Its lands and peoples were diverse, not a single modern nation-state.

The name “Holy Roman Empire” became familiar after Otto’s coronation.

overview.text: The Great Leap Forward was Mao Zedong's attempt to accelerate China's economic transformation beginning in 1958. Leaders tried to draw labor and resources from farming into ambitious industrial and construction efforts under central planning. The campaign placed enormous demands on rural workers while food production and distribution deteriorated. A devastating famine followed in 1959–1961, killing millions; scholars disagree about precise totals and the weight of different causes. Research emphasizes policy choices, including the diversion of agricultural resources to industry, rather than treating the disaster as a simple crop failure. The episode shows how official production goals could conceal severe shortages among the people expected to meet them.

The associated famine struck in 1959–1961.
Labor and resources were diverted from agriculture toward industrial aims.
The famine killed millions of people.
Scholars identify central planning and distribution choices among its causes.

overview.text: The United Nations is an international organization founded after World War II to help countries prevent conflict and cooperate on shared problems. Representatives signed its Charter in San Francisco on June 26, 1945, and it came into force on October 24. The Charter sets goals that include international peace, friendly relations, human rights, and cooperation. In the General Assembly, all member states have representation. The Security Council has special responsibility for peace and security; five states hold permanent seats and veto power, while ten others serve elected terms. These different bodies help explain why a global debate in the Assembly and a binding Council decision follow different rules.

The permanent members are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States.

overview.text: The Mau Mau uprising was an armed anti-colonial struggle in Kenya during the 1950s. African demands for land and political rights had grown under British rule, and fighters associated with the Kenya Land and Freedom Army drew especially from Gikuyu, Embu and Meru communities. The colonial government declared a state of emergency in October 1952 and answered the insurgency with military campaigns, mass detention and forced village relocation. Dedan Kimathi became a prominent forest fighter; his capture in 1956 weakened organized resistance. Violence affected civilians as well as combatants, and the emergency left enduring trauma. Kenya gained independence in 1963, after the armed rebellion itself had largely been defeated.

overview.text: The Spanish Inquisition was a system of religious tribunals established in the kingdoms ruled by Ferdinand and Isabella after a papal authorization in 1478. It investigated suspected heresy among baptized Christians, with early attention focused on conversos, Jews who had converted to Christianity and their descendants. Unlike earlier medieval inquisitions, the Spanish institution gave the monarchs strong control over appointments and administration. Its reach later included other groups and prohibited beliefs, while censorship became part of its work. Trials could involve imprisonment and public punishment, making religious conformity a matter of state power as well as church doctrine. The institution changed over time and lasted for centuries.

The institution later addressed other alleged heresies and censorship.

overview.text: The Great Emu War is the nickname for a 1932 Australian effort to protect wheat farms from emus in Western Australia. Large numbers of birds crossed fields and damaged crops and fences, so authorities sent a small Army detachment with machine guns to the Campion district. The soldiers found the fast-moving flocks difficult to target, and one gun jammed during an early encounter. The first operation stopped after about a week, then resumed in November and continued into December. Although birds were killed, the raids did not eliminate the crop problem. Calling it a “war” is a humorous shorthand for a wildlife-control campaign, not a conflict between armies.

overview.text: Enslaved people were human beings held under systems that denied their freedom and compelled their labor. In the Atlantic chattel-slavery system, law treated people as property that could be bought and sold. Captives from Africa endured the Middle Passage aboard crowded slave ships, often bound for plantations in the Caribbean and Brazil as well as North America. Enslavers tried to control work, movement and family life, but enslaved people resisted in many ways, from slowing work and seeking legal freedom to escape and revolt. Studying the institution requires seeing both the violence of forced labor and the choices and relationships of the people who lived through it. Forms of slavery differed across times and places.

Enslaved people resisted through actions including escape and rebellion.

overview.text: The Berlin Airlift supplied West Berlin during an early Cold War confrontation. On June 24, 1948, the Soviet Union blocked road, rail and water access from western-occupied Germany to the western sectors of Berlin. The United States and United Kingdom responded by flying in essentials, especially food and fuel, instead of abandoning the city. The American operation was called Operation Vittles; the British called theirs Plainfare. Aircraft used air corridors to keep deliveries moving through winter and into the next year. The blockade ended on May 12, 1949. The flight network had become more efficient, with planes arriving frequently at Berlin’s Tempelhof Airport. Its success demonstrated Western determination to sustain West Berlin without direct ground fighting.

overview.text: The Battle of Poltava was fought on July 8, 1709, near the city of Poltava in what is now Ukraine. During the Great Northern War, forces of Tsar Peter I of Russia defeated the Swedish army of King Charles XII. Ukrainian hetman Ivan Mazepa had allied with Charles in hopes of escaping Russian control, and he fled with the Swedish king after the defeat. The battle broke Sweden's offensive momentum and strengthened Russia's position in northern and eastern Europe. It was a turning point, not the war's final battle: fighting continued until 1721. Histories using different calendars may give a late-June date for the same event.
